# `Q-22-4` — Math Command Missing An Argument

> A math command was used with fewer arguments than it takes (`\frac{a}` has one, needs two), or a macro was called with the wrong number of arguments.

## What this means

Commands such as `\frac`, `\sqrt`, `\overset` and `\binom` take a fixed number of brace-delimited arguments, and a macro takes the number declared in its `\newcommand`. When an argument is missing, the command is emitted as an error at its position and the equation falls back to verbatim source in formats that need a conversion.

## Why this happens

Common causes: an unfinished edit (`\frac{a}` with the denominator still to write), a brace typed as a parenthesis (`\frac(a)(b)`), or a macro used with the wrong count (`\newcommand{\pr}[2]{…} \pr{x}`).

## How to fix it

Supply every argument in braces. Single characters may be given bare (`\frac12`), but anything longer needs `{…}`.

## Where it is reported

Math diagnostics point into the `.qmd` at the exact characters inside the
`$…$` or `$$…$$` block, including math that spans several lines or sits
inside a block quote or list item. When a `\newcommand` macro is involved,
a problem inside the macro body points at the definition and a problem in
a macro argument points at the use.
